newsitem.title: FRANCE: French railway chooses telecoms partner.
newsitem.headline: French railway chooses telecoms partner.

text.p: France's SNCF state railway said on Wednesday it had chosen Generale des Eaux unit Cegetel over rival bidders as an industrial partner to run its telecommunications network and help fund development.
Negotiations to complete the deal, which will see the privately owned operator inject funds into an SNCF subsidiary, will be completed by March 31, SNCF said in a statement.

The move, decided at a board meeting on Wednesday, came after a search for parthers was eventually narrowed down to Cegetel and a group led by French construction group Bouygues and its Italian partner STET.
The idea of granting Cegetel exclusive rights to the last lap of negotiations was to reach a firm accord with the group which made the best offer, SNCF said.
Cegetel is a joint venture between Generale des Eaux, British Telecom Plc and Mannesmann of Germany.
SNCF said it was bringing in an outsider to help pay for a vast network that has more capacity than the railway needs.
"It (SNCF) must develop and modernise the network and this needs large investments," it said without giving a figure.
Sensitive to the potential for unrest among employees who bitterly oppose rail reforms, SNCF said staff on the new network would maintain their special status as state railway employees.
SNCF started looking for investors after Telecommunications Minister Francois Fillon in December granted a 15-year telecoms operating licence to its Telecom Developpement unit (TD).

The licence covers the railroad's existing network of 8,000 kilometres of optic fibre all over the country, as well as radio links, which will be expanded to some 12,000 kilometres in the next six years, SNCF sources have said.

SNCF's lines have been hailed as a vital part in any operator's expansion plans, cutting the time needed to set up a network in time for European liberalisation in 1998 as well as reducing investment needs.
SNCF gave no financial details of the link-up, but Cegetel said proposals called for it to buy 49.9 percent of the capital of the TD subsidiary, with SNCF holding onto the majority share.
Cegetel said TD would become the sole network for its long-distance communications including traffic generated by its SFR mobile telephone network.
It said the system would be a "genuine alternative network for long-distance telecommunications" once the European market was thrown open to competition from January, 1998.
SNCF said TD would manage the network and a second company, TD Services (TDS), would sell the service to final consumers.
The blueprint also calls for SNCF's partner in TD to take a majority stake in TDS and apply its know-how there.
Both Generale des Eaux and Bouygues already run alternative mobile phone networks to the state supplier France Telecom.
A third offer had come from the Unisource consortium made up of Dutch KPN, Telia AB of Sweden, Swiss Telecom PTT and Spain's Telefonica. AT&T of the United States was also reported to be interested.

Telecom Developpement, like any future rival to France Telecom, will have to contribute to the costs of running the public service of telecommunications which will remain assured by the national operator. A first tranche of 20 percent in France Telecom is expected to be floated this spring.
